Write an email to a colleague about encouraging people to share what they know at work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Getting people to share what they know

Hi Sam,

I've been thinking about something we talked about last week: a lot of the knowledge on our team lives in just a few people's heads. When one of them is out sick or moves on, we feel it right away. I'd like us to do something about that.

Here's the core problem. People don't hold back knowledge because they're selfish. They hold back because sharing feels risky or thankless. Some worry that their expertise is the reason they're valued (if everyone knows what I know, am I still needed?). Others think what they know isn't interesting enough to share. And plenty of people are simply too busy to write anything down.

I think we can address all three, and I'd like to propose a few small steps.

First, let's make sharing visible and appreciated. When someone explains a process, answers a tough question, or documents a workaround, we should say thanks publicly, in the team channel and in our weekly meeting. Energy grows when people feel appreciated, and recognition is the cheapest way I know to get more of the behavior we want.

Second, let's lower the effort. Nobody needs to write a polished guide. A ten-minute "show and tell" at the end of our Thursday meeting, or a rough page in the wiki, is plenty. We can always clean it up later. I'd rather have a messy note than a perfect one that never gets written.

Third, let's reframe expertise. Knowing something is useful, but teaching it is what makes someone a leader. If we treat sharing as a sign of mastery rather than a threat to job security, people will feel more comfortable doing it. I'd be glad to go first and share a couple of things I've learned the hard way, so it's clear that imperfect contributions are welcome.

Finally, let's make it part of the work, not an extra. If we expect people to share but give them no time, it won't happen. Maybe we can set aside an hour every other week for it.

Would you be willing to try this for a month and see what happens? I'm happy to put together a short plan and bring it to the next meeting. Let me know what you think, or grab me for a quick chat if that's easier.

Thanks,
[name]
